rows.why: S1 expects a bounty of 10000 with the default share to release 7500 and leave the task 'partially released'. No item asks what the default share is or what passing the hidden tests should release. Item 1 is about rounding and item 3 is about which share values are valid and in what unit, so neither settles this.

Item 1 asks how the hidden-test share is rounded. The pick rounds down using BigInt integer division and gives the remainder to UAT, so the two always add up to the bounty and stay exact up to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. The run splitBounty(101,7500) → {75,26} matches the scenario's 999 → 749 and 250.

S3 is the normal path: after the hidden-test share is released, UAT releases the rest and the task becomes 'fully released'. Item 8 asks whether 'remaining balance' means bounty minus the computed share or a figure read from the store. Both readings give the same amount in this scenario, so answering item 8 would not change what S3 expects.

Item 7 asks what a failed hidden-test run does to the state. The task does stay 'locked' with no releases. The pick says nothing is saved, but the run shows writesAfterFail: 1, so the handler does write state to the store on a failed run. The scenario says nothing is recorded.

Item 6 asks what happens when UAT is approved before the hidden tests pass. The run rejects with 'cannot approve UAT: the hidden tests have not passed' and makes 0 writes, which is what the scenario expects.
Item 9 asks how a zero-bounty task behaves. The status is 'pro bono' as expected, but the run records releases of amount 0 for hidden-tests and uat. The scenario says no release is ever recorded.

Item 5 covers both a redelivered event id and a new event of the same kind after the release. The pick leaves the state unchanged and writes nothing. The run shows a second hidden-tests-passed with a different id still gives one release and writes: 1 in total.

Item 11 asks how concurrent events are handled. The pick runs events one at a time through a promise queue, so the second event sees the first one's saved state. Together with the idempotency in item 5, that gives exactly one release for simultaneous duplicates. The run does not exercise concurrency, so this rests on the stated design.

Item 11 also covers store failures. The run shows the first handle rejecting with the store's 'boom' error and leaving the state unset. Handling the same event again then succeeds with a single 75 release, which is what the scenario expects.
